### How many and what things are required so that a relation is real on the part of both termini. Cap. CLXXXI.

Regarding the sixth, namely, what are required for a real relation which is so real that it also has an opposite relation corresponding to it in the opposite terminus, and thus, according to mutual correspondence from either terminus, they are real. It must be said that the four conditions aforementioned are immediate, and with these, one other, which is the fifth, and this regards both relations and both termini, namely that each relation be of the same order. Doctors call this condition "being of the same order," because if the relation of one extreme is infinite and outside of every genus, the relation of the opposite extreme must similarly be of the same order and condition, such that it is likewise infinite, unlimited, and outside of every genus. And this is found in divine relations. For just as the relation whereby the Father is related to the Son is outside of every genus, so is the relation whereby the Son is related to the Father. Hence they mutually correspond to each other in this, that is, being outside of every genus and being infinite and unlimited. Or they are also said to be of the same order if one is finite and within a genus, that the relation of the opposite extreme is similarly of the same condition. And in that way, in human matters, the relation of father to son and the relation of son to father are of the same genus and order. And because the relation of God to the creature is not of the same order as the relation of the creature to God, therefore it cannot be a real relation according to mutual correspondence on the part of both extremes.

From this it follows that, although the Pope and the prince are released from human laws, <note>reference: c. Proposuit, De concessio. preb. l Princeps. ff. De legi.</note> this is to be understood only regarding coercive force, but not regarding directive force, to which they are entirely subject: as the saintly Thomas teaches in 1. 2. q. 90. art. 1. This is in agreement with what Pope Hadrian hands down in his 4th book of Sentences on the matter of restitution, and Cardinal, conf. 142, Roman conf. 360, around the beginning, col. 7, verse "Thirdly I ask." Abb. in c. Ad decorem De insti. Moderni in c. Quae in ecclesiarum, De constitu. Many examples could be assigned for this, but this discussion belongs elsewhere; for it concerns the maintenance or abrogation of laws and that vast matter of dispensations, about which we shall perhaps treat elsewhere, for that dispute is very difficult and dangerous, and in which many have discussed much, but which is found to be explored with little attention by most professors of canon law; while they treat these laws—divine, natural, and human—very negligently, using many allegations from here and there that are ill-applied. Finally, there are, as we have said, in the fourth place, certain deductions which, even if they consist of reason and are even called determinations of natural law, are nevertheless so far removed from the first truths that sometimes it does not appear whether they follow from them or rather are repugnant to them; for instance, that he who sins should be punished by such a penalty or such another; whom, however, we are taught by natural law ought entirely to be punished. For my part, I only wish</meta> that I might enjoy the sight of this city, which I have saved, with a calm and quiet mind. What if I do not ask for this? What if my former labor, my anxiety, my efforts, and my vigils remain at the service of my friends and are available to all? If neither my friends in the <term>forum</term> <gloss>public square/marketplace</gloss> nor the <term>Respublica</term> <gloss>Republic/State</gloss> in the <term>curia</term> <gloss>Senate house</gloss> miss my attention; if I am claimed by labor not only by a respite from past deeds, but by neither the excuse of honor nor age; if my will, my industry, my home, my spirit, and my ears are open to all; if I am left with no time even to record and reflect upon those things which I accomplished for the safety of all: will this still be called a kingdom? No one can be found who would wish to be the deputy of such a ruler. The suspicion of a kingdom is far removed. If you ask who at Rome have attempted to seize a kingdom, you will find them within your own family portraits without having to unfold the memory of the annals. For my own achievements, I suppose, have exalted me too much and have brought me I know not what arrogance. Concerning these matters, which are so clear and so immortal, judges, I can say this: that I, who rescued this city and the lives of all citizens from the greatest dangers, would be satisfied if, from this great benefit conferred upon all mortals, no danger were to redound upon me. For I remember in what state I performed such great deeds, and I understand in what city I live. The <term>forum</term> <gloss>public square</gloss> is full of those men whom I drove away from your necks, judges, yet I have not removed them from my own. Unless, indeed, you think there were few who could attempt or hope that they could destroy such a great empire. I was able to snatch the torches and pull the swords from the hands of these men, as I did. Yet I could neither cure nor remove their wicked and nefarious intentions. They think that this cause of yours is surpassed by you. But if we seem like foreigners to you, whose name and honor have already become established both in this city and in the reputation and discourse of men, how much more necessarily must those competitors of yours seem like foreigners to you, who have been chosen from all over Italy and now contend with you for honor and for every dignity? Beware of calling any one of them a foreigner, lest you be overwhelmed by the votes of foreigners. For if they bring strength and industry, believe me, they will shake off this posturing of yours and will often rouse you from your slumber. They will not allow themselves to be surpassed in honor by you, unless they are surpassed by virtue. And if, judges, it were necessary that I and you <note>referring to the jury or the noble class</note> seem like foreigners to the other patricians, this fault would nonetheless be silenced by Torquatus <note>Lucius Manlius Torquatus</note>. For he himself is from a municipal town on his mother’s side, of a most honorable and noble family, but still, he is from Asculum. Therefore, let him either teach that the people of Picenum alone are not foreigners, or let him rejoice that I do not place my own origin ahead of his. Therefore, do not call me a foreigner hereafter, lest you be more severely refuted; and do not call me a King, lest you be mocked. Unless, perhaps, it seems kingly to you to live in such a way that you serve no man, nor even any desire; to despise all lusts; to feel no need for gold, silver, or other such things; to hold opinions freely in the Senate; to consult the utility of the people rather than their will; to yield to no one, and to stand against many. If you think this is kingly, I confess that I am a King. But if my power, if my dominance, if finally any arrogant or proud statement moves you, why do you not bring that forward, rather than the jealousy of a word and the insult of a slur? If, having performed such great services for the Republic, I were to ask for no other reward from the Senate and the Roman people than an honorable retirement, who would not grant it? Let them keep for themselves their honors, their commands, their provinces, their triumphs, and the other illustrious badges of glory.

<summary>Cicero defends his status as a Roman citizen and his public service against the accusations of Torquatus, arguing that his independence and dedication to the state constitute true nobility rather than tyrannical "kingly" ambition.</summary>

### On the nature of gold

**S**hould one object to these points concerning the nature of gold, which alone, according to <term>Hermes</term> <gloss>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary sage of alchemy</gloss>, is the metal in which no sickness appears. For neither part of its material is infected or intemperate. Since, like all other metals, it is composed of sulfur and quicksilver, its sulfur is most lucid and clean, and, having been brought to purity through the most powerful washings, it possesses no combustible greasiness at all, nor any watery, phlegmatic humidity capable of evaporation. It has been sublimated and digested in concave places where the solid surface is often <unclear>sublimated and digested by a temperate</unclear> heat, in a digestion process that is called <term>pepasis</term> <gloss>maturation</gloss>. The earthy substance that is incorporated into the sulfur is clean, very subtle, and suspended vaporously throughout the entire substance of the radical moisture of that sulfur. Because of this, it follows that the heat of that sulfur is constitutional, departing in no way from temperament; and this is like the masculine virtue in the composition of gold. Similarly, its quicksilver has two substances cleansed to the extremes. For the third element, which is in the heat itself, is subtilized, not only materially divided, but is most subtle vaporously, having been often sublimated in the cavities of the earth by the life-giving heat of the sun and the stars. Similarly, the watery element is also subtilized in the same manner of repeated subtilization, and since glass is present in this way, it is subtilized finely. It is evident that when mixed together by heat and the disposition of the place that fosters and reflects the vapor upon itself, they are bound together by the most powerful bond of mixture. Sulfur does not enter into the composition of gold merely by quality, but by substance, and since it is a subtle substance, it will penetrate everywhere through the quicksilver, and by coagulating, it colors it. And since both are brought by sublimation to the form of the superior elements, which in the nature of transparency arrive with a perpetual body, each will have full purity. And when many parts of the matter are thickened, they will stand together; this indeed is a property of a subtle substance, that standing together through coagulation, it will have many parts in a very small space. Therefore, the contracted transparency will make a citrine color, and the subtlety makes great solidification, and the constancy of many parts together in a small place and position makes weight, just as is proven from those things which have been reasonably demonstrated in the *Physics* and the *De Caelo*. It follows, however, from the solidification and temperament together that gold is little evaporable or not at all; therefore, it is almost odorless. Although an odor is not essentially a smoky evaporation, a strong odor is nevertheless frequently found with a smoky evaporation, because of which it further follows that gold is more incorruptible than any metal and more resistant to fire because of the strongest commixtion of its mixture. For a smoky evaporation indicates a certain corruption of bodies, which is less in silver and more in copper. From these, we have the reason why those things that do not burn gold, such as sulfur and arsenic and certain others, do burn silver. The cause of this

From the temperance of gold, it is understood why it is hot and moist, conferring relief to the trembling of the heart and to melancholy, which makes one sad. The great purity of the matter makes it so that it is very rarely found mixed with other bodies, but is always almost pure, which, when it is mixed with others, cannot retain such purity, and for this reason, it degenerates into copper. This vessel, placed in the fire, does not break in the fire by sensible consumption. Nevertheless, the clay of the wise is prepared in another way in alchemical texts, but that which goldsmiths use suffices here. # Red metals, however, are different in their color and mixture from those already mentioned: as we have sufficiently shown when we dealt with the colors of metals.

Iron has a specific nature of its own beyond the other elements. Let us therefore speak of the composition of **copper** <note>original: "eris"; here referring to copper or its alloys</note>, assuming what has long been proven: that every metal is composed of **sulfur** and **quicksilver** <note>original: "argento vivo"; mercury</note>. Let us suppose that the quicksilver is good and not dreggy or muddy, yet not entirely purged of external moisture. Let the substance of the sulfur be dreggy, burning, and partially ignited, just as it is mixed with the quicksilver in substance and quality. For now, without doubt, it turns the quicksilver red; because both are not fully refined, they cannot mix well. Then it creates copper, which is not of an entirely good mixture. Because of this, much of it is consumed and much evaporates in the fire, since the sulfur is partially burnt. Therefore, some parts of the quicksilver are purified more than others, and the superfluous moisture in them is consumed; in those parts, it will seem to have **veins of gold**. In other parts, however, where it is less "digested" <term>digestio; the natural "cooking" or ripening of minerals in the earth</term>, it will be scaly, base, and earthy due to the burning. We have clearly found this diversity in the copper found in the German regions, in the place called <margin>Goslar</margin> **Goslar**. Therefore, this copper is esteemed better than all others, as if having veins of gold mixed in. It is not improbable that the sulfur of that copper is mixed with red **arsenic** in some quantity, and therefore the sulfur of that metal is more "burning" than that of others.

<margin>Copper is turned into brass</margin>
Now we know the material of copper: it is a metal made from quicksilver, having a bit more than is proper through the mixture of burning sulfur, which leads it to a red form. The nature by which sulfur is "burning" has been sufficiently determined in what preceded. **Arsenic**, when calcined <note>heated to a high temperature to remove volatile substances</note>, turns black from red; but afterward, when **sublimated** <note>turned into vapor and then solidified</note> in an **alutel** <note>original: "alutel"; a pear-shaped vessel used in alchemy for sublimation</note>, which is a covered vessel with a high neck as we have often said, it returns white like snow. If such calcination and sublimation are repeated often, it becomes very white and very sharp. Because of this sharpness, when joined to copper by melting, it penetrates it and turns it white. However, if it stays in the fire a long time, the copper will "breathe out" the arsenic, and then the original color of the copper returns, as is easily proven in alchemical works. Those who work much with copper in our regions—namely in Paris, Cologne, and other places where I have been and seen experiments—turn copper into **brass** <note>original: "auricalcum"; orichalcum</note> by using the powder of a stone called **calamine** <note>zinc ore</note>. When the stone evaporates, a dim splendor still remains, inclining somewhat toward the appearance of gold. To make it whiter and thus more similar to the yellow of gold, they mix in a little **tin**. Because of this, the brass loses much of the ductility <note>the ability to be hammered thin or drawn into wire</note> of the copper. Those who wish to deceive and induce a splendor similar to gold "bind" the stone so that it remains longer in the copper in the fire and does not evaporate quickly.

It is "bound" by **glass oil**: fragments of glass are toasted and turned into powder, which is sprinkled into the crucible over the copper after the calamine has been put in. Then the melted glass floats over the copper and does not allow the stone or its virtue to evaporate; instead, it reflects the vapor of the stone back into the copper. Thus, for a while, it strongly purges the copper and burns away the dreggy materials in it. Eventually, however, even the glass oil evaporates, and then the virtue of the stone evaporates; but the brass is made much more splendid than it would be without it. He who intends to make it resemble gold even more repeats these purgings with the glass oil often, and in place of tin, he takes **silver** and mixes it with the brass. This makes it so ruddy and yellow in color that many believe it to be gold, though in truth it remains in the species of copper.

<margin>Hermes</margin>
**Hermes** <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary founder of alchemy</note> says that if powdered **tutty** <note>original: "tuchia"; zinc oxide collected from smelting furnaces</note>, whether white or red, is added to melted copper, it converts it to the color of gold. What tutty is will be discussed in the following book where we deal with intermediate substances. But let it suffice here that by the "burning" of the tutty, the earthiness is removed and it purges the copper of its superfluous moisture; therefore, it will then be more beautiful. However, the virtue of the tutty also evaporates through fire if it stands in the fire for a long time. Unless another "medicine" <note>an additive or reagent</note> is used, the tutty will evaporate, and then the original color of the copper returns. Hermes also says, and experience agrees, that if such copper is sprinkled with vinegar or the urine of a virgin male child, the virtue of the urine or vinegar will penetrate the substance of the copper and turn it green. If, however, the copper is placed by itself over pressed grape skins, it will be converted into an excellent, shining green color by the vapor of the wine alone. But if **orpiment** <note>original: "auripigmentum"; a yellow arsenic ore</note> or arsenic is brought near this color, especially if it is burnt, it destroys the green and induces a dark, earthy color inclining toward opacity. The cause of this is easily shown from what has been said. For salt is opening, and therefore it opens the substance of the copper, especially if it has been hammered into thin plates; then the sharp vapor of the vinegar or urine ignites it, which comes from the overly-ignited sulfur. Because of this, the light earthy moisture joined to it, which is ignited, takes on that greenness, much like the hottest and worst bile which physicians call the "rust of copper." Since at first the vapor is not as sharp as the vapor of joined wine, it does not induce such an intense redness, and so the gold color remains pleasant. Orpiment, however, is excellently "burning," and so when it approaches a substance colored this way, it burns the small amount of moisture in it; then what remains is the earthy opacity. This is the same way that burnt bile leaves behind a "melancholic ash," according to medical experience. Thus, so much has been said concerning the nature and effects of copper.
